justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish but essentially range-bound view on the underlying asset priced near 370. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing market price, assuming no major catalysts were imminent and that short-term momentum and mean-reversion forces would largely offset each other, producing only a marginal drift upward to 370.5. At the 1-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 372, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run equity risk premium embedded in prices, while acknowledging that weekly moves are dominated by noise rather than fundamentals. For the 1-month horizon, the 375 estimate reflects a continuation of that same modest drift, consistent with roughly 1–2% expected monthly appreciation in a stable macro environment, without assuming any strong directional catalyst.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons in a manner roughly consistent with the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility. At the 1-day level, realized volatility in the asset suggested a daily standard deviation in the range of 7–8 points, so a 90% interval spanning about 25 points total is plausible. Over a week, multi-day volatility compounds and path dependency introduces additional uncertainty, widening the band to roughly 44 points. Over a month, macroeconomic data releases, earnings, central bank decisions, and geopolitical developments all accumulate, justifying a 90-point-wide interval for the monthly forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise central bank policy shift — an emergency rate cut or hike — which could easily move prices 5–10% in a single session, well outside the 1-day range. A major geopolitical shock, credit event, or liquidity crisis could similarly break the monthly interval on the downside. On the upside, an unexpected dovish pivot combined with strong economic data could trigger a rapid repricing that pushes prices above 420 within the month.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions with stationary volatility, which is a simplification. In reality, volatility clusters and fat tails mean that extreme outcomes are more probable than a Gaussian model implies. Periods of market stress tend to produce correlation breakdowns and liquidity gaps that make even wide confidence intervals look narrow in hindsight. Readers should treat these forecasts as a central tendency with acknowledged model risk, not as a precise probabilistic guarantee.
